label: Morning edition
summary: Keanu, **Democrats won the House and the Senate** in a midterm wave, with Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina flipping in the Senate (NPR, NBC, CNN). Trump says he is "absolutely willing to accept" the results but will veto "insane" bills, and he blamed Fox News and Gov. Greg Abbott (Axios, Fox News). Conservative writers at the Free Press and National Review blame tariffs, weak nominees and Trump's treatment of Congress (The Free Press, National Review). In California, **Prop 40 is failing** with about 56% no while Prop 42 leads, and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra won in a landslide (CalMatters, KQED, SF Chronicle). **Bay Area transit won big** with the regional sales tax near 61% and Muni's Prop H near 73% (SF Chronicle, KQED). Trump says there is "no rush" on Iran strikes as Doha talks continue, and U.S.-mediated Ukraine talks are set for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi (Axios, CNBC, The Hill). Futures rebounded after the sweep, but **AI data center stocks slid** on Hinojosa's Texas win, with CoreWeave down 7% and Oracle 4.3% (CNBC, Bloomberg). A **December Fed hike is still about 75% priced** with inflation at 3.7% (NPR, CNBC). Anthropic's IPO roadshow could start the week of Nov. 9 (Bloomberg). NASA's Swift telescope was due to re-enter near **12:30 a.m. Pacific** (NASA, Space.com).

Prop 40 billionaire tax is failing as Prop 42 leads.

stories.title: Democrats win the House and the Senate in a midterm wave
stories.summary: NPR, NBC and CNN project full Democratic control of Congress, with Senate seats flipping in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina.
story: NPR, NBC News and CNN projected Tuesday night that Democrats won both chambers of Congress. NPR, using Associated Press calls, said Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. CNN's tally put the Senate at 54 Democratic seats to 44 Republican, with Alaska and Mississippi still uncalled. In the House, NBC projected at least 258 Democratic seats, the most since 1993. Axios called it a blue tsunami.

Republicans began the year holding the Senate 53 to 47, and Democrats needed a net gain of four seats. NPR said few expected that majority to be at risk. Fox News reported that James Talarico beat Ken Paxton in Texas and that Abdul El-Sayed won the open Michigan seat over Mike Rogers. NBC reported that Troy Jackson beat Susan Collins in Maine. In Mississippi, NPR said only 28 votes separated Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith from Democrat Scott Colom, who was ahead.

Exit polls pointed to the cost of living and government corruption as top issues (NBC News). The Washington Examiner reported that affordability mattered to 89% of voters and that voters preferred Democrats on every issue except immigration. NBC said 43% of voters cited opposition to Trump as one reason they voted. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said, 'We ran on affordability, we won on affordability and now it's our job to govern on affordability' (NPR). Senate Republican leader John Thune said his conference will not stand idly by (NBC).

The win has limits. Trump keeps his veto, so most Democratic bills cannot become law without his signature (NPR). Axios noted that nearly 6 in 10 Democratic-leaning voters told CBS News/YouGov their vote was about stopping Trump, which suggests the result reflects opposition more than support for a Democratic program. A Democratic Senate also halts the steady confirmation of Trump's judges (NPR).
stories.flag: Alaska and Mississippi Senate races and dozens of House races were uncalled; outlets differ on seat totals.
facts: NPR, NBC and CNN project Democrats won both the House and the Senate.
CNN's Senate tally: 54 Democratic seats, 44 Republican, Alaska and Mississippi uncalled.
NBC projects at least 258 House seats for Democrats, the most since 1993.
Republicans had held the Senate 53 to 47 (NPR).
Gina Hinojosa also defeated Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (Axios, CNBC).
stories.left: Voters rejected a presidency that raised their costs through tariffs and an unpopular war while the White House pursued enforcement and loyalty over affordability. Democrats ran on prices and corruption and earned a mandate to investigate and to block harmful policy. The result shows that a message about everyday costs can win in deep red Ohio, Kansas and Texas. Now they must show they can lower costs, not only oppose Trump.
stories.right: Midterms punish the president's party, and this one was worsened by weak nominees, high gas prices tied to the Iran war and tariffs that voters felt at the register. Conservatives should read the result as a warning about governing without consensus, not as a rejection of border security or lower taxes, where exit polls still favored Republicans on immigration. Democrats now own the congressional agenda, and their base will demand impeachment-style fights that can reunite the right.
stories.next: New senators and members are sworn in in January; Alaska and Mississippi Senate calls and the final House count come as ballots are tallied.

stories.title: Trump says he will accept the results, vows vetoes and blames Fox News
stories.summary: Trump told the New York Times he is 'absolutely willing' to accept the results, then promised to veto 'insane' Democratic bills.
story: President Trump said he would accept the midterm results and also promised to use his veto. He told the New York Times he is 'absolutely willing to accept those results,' and CNN reported that this shut down, for now, questions about whether he would contest the outcome. He told Fox News, 'They'll send over things that are insane and I'll veto them' (Fox News, Axios, CNN).

Axios reported that Trump said Republicans lost because he was not on the ballot and that he was a little bit surprised by the scale of the defeat. He blamed Fox News, which Axios said he did without evidence, and blamed Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Fox News also reported that Trump pointed to gas prices tied to the Iran conflict as a factor and said some candidates alienated his base by opposing him earlier.

There were mixed signals on cooperation. Trump told Politico he is eager to strike deals instead of spending his last two years on vetoes, and told the Wall Street Journal he and Republicans would work with Democrats, per CNBC's market coverage. CNBC tied a jump in Dow futures of about 1,083 points to his acceptance of the results.
Whether the two sides find any common ground will depend on how fast House Democrats move on oversight and on what Trump is willing to trade for his veto.
facts: Trump told the New York Times he is 'absolutely willing to accept those results.'
He told Fox News Democrats will send 'insane' bills and he will veto them.
Axios said he blamed Fox News without evidence and said Republicans lost because he was not on the ballot.
Abbott called Hinojosa to concede (Axios, Fox News).
Dow futures jumped about 2.1% on his acceptance, per CNBC.
stories.left: Accepting the result is the minimum a president owes the voters, and the history of attacks on elections makes it worth noting. Blaming Fox News and Abbott avoids the obvious cause, an unpopular agenda on tariffs, the Iran war and immigration enforcement. A veto pledge before any bill exists signals that he plans to govern by confrontation. Democrats should test his offer to deal with concrete affordability bills.
stories.right: The president did the right thing by accepting the result, and his veto is the constitutional check that divided government was designed to give him. Voters in 2026 punished the party in power for prices, and conservatives are right to ask whether nominees like Paxton cost winnable seats. A president willing to deal on lower costs and border security can still shape the next two years, and Democrats who overreach with impeachment will hand him leverage.
stories.next: Watch for the first Trump-Jeffries and Trump-Thune meetings and the lame-duck session before the new Congress takes over in January.

stories.title: Conservative writers blame Trump and weak nominees for the Republican wipeout
stories.summary: The Free Press, National Review and the Washington Examiner describe a 'bloodbath' and point to tariffs, Trump's treatment of Congress and candidates like Ken Paxton.
story: Conservative outlets gave unusually sharp post-mortems. The Free Press ran 'Wipeout,' describing the night as a '100-year flood' for Republicans, and Eli Lake argued in 'How Trump Blew It' that Trump squandered the gains of his 2024 comeback. National Review published 'Trump's Disregard for Congress Contributed to Republicans' Midterm Defeat.' The Washington Examiner reported the party was grappling with an electoral 'bloodbath.'

The Examiner also reported that Trump allies were searching for scapegoats. A former Trump spokeswoman quoted by the Examiner blamed tariffs that raised costs and immigration enforcement. Another Examiner column said nominating Paxton in an already poor environment showed Republican arrogance. Exit polls the Examiner cited showed Democrats with an edge on nearly every issue, with immigration the exception.

There was dissent from the idea that this was only about Trump. Axios, in a separate analysis, warned that Democrats could learn the wrong lesson from a blowout, since voter opinion of their party remains weak. Fox News carried a Liz Peek column arguing the defeat may have a silver lining for Republicans.

What conservatives do next matters for 2028. Some of these writers want a break from unilateral executive action and a return to working with Congress, while Trump's own circle is blaming Fox News and Abbott.
facts: The Free Press called the night a '100-year flood' for Republicans.
National Review argued Trump's treatment of congressional Republicans contributed to the loss.
The Washington Examiner reported Trump allies searching for scapegoats.
Examiner-cited exit polls showed Democrats ahead on every issue except immigration.
Axios warned Democrats could misread a blowout win.
stories.left: The right's own press is saying what Democrats argued all year: tariffs, an unpopular war and a president who treats Congress with contempt cost Republicans the country. The honest lesson is that voters wanted lower prices and less chaos. Democrats should take care to hear the affordability message and not claim a mandate for every progressive priority.
stories.right: A thoughtful conservative reading is that the movement won in 2024 on prices and the border and then lost in 2026 by drifting from both. Weak nominees, executive-order governing and tariff-driven costs are fixable errors. The path back is candidate quality, working through Congress, and a message on affordability that makes voters trust Republicans again.
stories.next: Watch how Senate Republicans choose leadership and whether Trump's attacks on Fox News and Abbott widen the party's rift.

stories.title: House Democrats weigh investigations first and impeachment later
stories.summary: Jeffries has not ruled impeachment in or out, and reporters say probes of Trump's businesses and immigration enforcement come first.
story: With the House won, Democrats are deciding how aggressively to use oversight. Fox News reported before the vote that House Democrats planned probes of Trump's family business dealings and Cabinet. Jeffries has said Democrats 'haven't ruled anything in, and we haven't ruled anything out' on impeachment, per Fox News. Schumer has said two years is too far away to predict (Fox News).

NBC News reported that Jeffries said the party should focus on the cost of living and not retribution, and that oversight is expected to be a priority. NBC also noted that some Democrats have vowed to impeach Trump a third time. The Washington Examiner earlier listed likely targets, including immigration enforcement tactics and the Epstein files.

Fox News also reported that Democrats are split on whether to pursue impeachment or the 25th Amendment, and on timing. Removal would need 67 Senate votes, which the Examiner has called unlikely even with a larger Democratic caucus.
DNC chair Ken Martin told NPR Democrats have 'great leverage' after the sweep, and NPR said the Senate win halts Trump's judicial confirmations.
stories.flag: Several of the Fox News and Examiner reports on Democratic plans were written before election night and describe intentions, not votes.
facts: Jeffries says nothing is ruled in or out on impeachment (Fox News).
Schumer called two years too far away to predict (Fox News).
Planned probe targets include Trump family businesses and immigration enforcement (Fox News, Washington Examiner).
Democrats are divided over impeachment versus the 25th Amendment (Fox News).
DNC chair Ken Martin says Democrats have 'great leverage' (NPR).
stories.left: Oversight is a core job of Congress, and a Republican Congress largely declined to do it. Probing conflicts of interest, immigration tactics and the Epstein files is accountability, not revenge. Leaders are right to put affordability first and let evidence decide on impeachment.
stories.right: Republicans see a Democratic majority eager to turn oversight into an impeachment campaign that distracts from prices, the issue that won them the election. Conservatives argue that investigating the president's family and Cabinet before passing any relief will look like the retribution Jeffries says he opposes. A third impeachment would fail in the Senate and energize Trump's base.
stories.next: New committee chairs and subpoena plans will start taking shape when the new Congress convenes in January; watch for early statements from Jeffries on impeachment.

stories.title: California's Prop 40 billionaire tax is failing while Prop 42 leads
stories.summary: Early returns show Prop 40 with about 56% no votes, and its counter-measure Prop 42 ahead at about 55%.
story: California voters appear to have rejected the Prop 40 billionaire tax. CalMatters, citing the Associated Press, reported it trailing with about 56% voting no with 54% of ballots counted, and KQED reported nearly 57% no on Tuesday night. Prop 42, the billionaire-backed measure that would ban wealth taxes, led with about 55% yes, and Prop 41 was failing with more than 52% no (CalMatters, KQED, SF Chronicle).

The measures interact. If Prop 40 got more votes than both 41 and 42, the tax would take effect. If either outpolls Prop 40, the tax does not. The union behind Prop 40, SEIU-UHW, seemed to concede early but said it would try again in 2028 if the Legislature 'fails to deliver a real solution' on health care funding. Union president Dave Regan said, 'That's not a hypothetical. That's our plan' (CalMatters).

The campaign was costly. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition and gave about $102 million to a committee he founded, per CalMatters. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Prop 40 and endorsed Prop 42. The California Democratic Party had endorsed the tax, splitting with Newsom (KQED, CalMatters). A late-October PPIC poll had shown support at 46% to 52% opposed.
The counts are not final. The SF Chronicle said nearly half of the state's projected vote remained uncounted at 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, and counting can run about a week.
stories.flag: Results are early and incomplete; Prop 40's final margin and Props 41 and 42 rankings could shift as ballots are counted.
stories.blindspot: No right-leaning outlet coverage of the results turned up in my search; coverage came from CalMatters, KQED and the SF Chronicle.
facts: Prop 40 was losing with about 56% no on early returns (CalMatters citing AP).
Prop 42 led with about 55% yes; Prop 41 trailed with more than 52% no.
Sergey Brin gave about $102 million to oppose the tax (CalMatters).
SEIU-UHW said it will try again in 2028 (CalMatters).
Gov. Newsom endorsed Prop 42.
stories.left: Supporters argued that a one-time 5% levy on about 200 billionaires was the most direct way to fund Medi-Cal and health care after federal cuts. They note that a record donor spent more than $100 million to defeat it, which they say shows how much power concentrated wealth has over California politics. The 46% yes in the final poll shows a large audience for taxing extreme wealth, and the union's 2028 vow keeps the question alive.
stories.right: Opponents argued the tax would drive founders and capital out of California, as Brin's own move out of state illustrated, and erode the income-tax base that funds the state. The SF Chronicle reported allegations against the campaign's architect, which he denies, and noted that top Democrats including Newsom opposed the tax. A one-time tax on unrealized wealth invites court challenges, and voters seem to agree that California should fix spending before taxing a few individuals.
stories.next: County registrars keep counting for roughly a week; certification is later in the month, and the Legislature faces the union's 2028 warning on health care funding.

stories.title: Bay Area voters approve a regional transit sales tax and a Muni parcel tax
stories.summary: Early returns show the regional measure winning with about 61% and San Francisco's Prop H with about 73%, a major relief for BART, Muni, Caltrain and AC Transit.
story: Bay Area voters approved new transit funding on election night. The SF Chronicle and KQED reported the regional measure (Prop RTM) winning with about 61% of the vote, above the simple majority it needed. It adds a half-cent sales tax in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties and a one-cent tax in San Francisco, and is expected to raise about $1 billion a year for BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit and other agencies. The tax runs for 14 years.

San Francisco's Prop H, a Muni parcel tax, led with roughly 72% to 73% yes and would raise about $184 million a year for 15 years, per KQED. The Chronicle said nearly 65% of the Alameda County sales tax money would go to BART operations, which matters for Fremont riders. KQED's headline said a transit 'death spiral' was averted.

The campaign had a fight. The Committee for Affordable Bay Area Transit argued that agencies exaggerated service cuts, that sales taxes are regressive and that the measure lacks accountability. An opposition spokesperson told the Chronicle that supporters were 'bamboozling voters.' Opponents had not conceded as of the reports.
The agencies said earlier that without new money they faced deep cuts, including station closures at BART. The money is expected to begin flowing next year.
stories.flag: Early returns; the Chronicle and KQED gave different Muni revenue totals ($332 million with both measures vs. $184 million a year for Prop H).
stories.blindspot: Coverage found came from the SF Chronicle and KQED, both left-leaning; no right-leaning outlet coverage turned up.
facts: The regional measure was winning with about 61% of the vote (SF Chronicle, KQED).
It levies a half-cent sales tax in four counties and one cent in San Francisco for 14 years.
It is expected to raise about $1 billion a year (SF Chronicle).
Prop H led with about 72% to 73% (SF Chronicle, KQED).
Opponents called sales taxes regressive and have not conceded.
stories.left: Transit is a public good that cuts emissions, congestion and household costs, and a region this rich should not let BART shrink. A sales tax is not ideal, but the Legislature would not give the region a fairer tool. The result shows voters will pay for service when they can see what it buys.
stories.right: Skeptics point out that sales taxes fall hardest on lower-income residents and that agencies have not shown they can run leaner. Ridership has not recovered to pre-pandemic levels, and critics want audits, fare enforcement and spending controls before more revenue. Voters approved the money, so the proof now has to come in on service levels.
stories.next: Watch for the first allocations to BART, Muni, Caltrain and AC Transit next year and for final certified totals in the coming weeks.

stories.title: Trump says 'no rush' on resuming Iran strikes as Doha talks continue
stories.summary: Axios, CNBC and Fox News report Iranian and Qatari mediators in Doha, a draft confidence-building sequence and a president who has not ruled out more strikes.
story: President Trump told Axios on Nov. 2 there is 'no rush' to decide whether to bomb Iran again. Iranian negotiators held a third straight day of talks with Qatari mediators in Doha on Nov. 1, aimed at ending the war (CNBC, citing Reuters). Iran and Qatar developed a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of an agreement with Washington (CNBC).

Fox News reported the U.S. launched 'defensive' strikes on an Iranian island as the talks hung in the balance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not yet made a choice on resuming military action (Fox News, Oct. 31). Trump has said he would not strike before the vote but has not ruled out action afterward. Qatari mediators drafted a three-day sequence of confidence-building steps to restart direct talks and awaited feedback from both sides, regional sources told reporters.

NPR reported Gulf states fear renewed war after the midterms. CNBC reported oil fell sharply on Monday on peace hopes, though reports on the size of the drop varied, and Trump claimed a record one-day drop of nearly $10 a barrel on his own account. WTI was at $94.88, down 1.26%, in the latest quote.
With the election over, the White House no longer has the midterm calendar as a reason to delay a decision, and analysts and Gulf diplomats expect a choice soon.
stories.flag: Reports differ on the size of Monday's oil drop (more than 7% in one CNBC headline, about 1% in another); the Trump claim of a record $10 drop is his own.
facts: Trump told Axios there is 'no rush' to decide on bombing Iran again.
Iranian and Qatari negotiators met in Doha for a third straight day on Nov. 1 (CNBC).
A proposal could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days of a deal (CNBC).
Qatar drafted a three-day confidence-building sequence (regional sources).
WTI crude is $94.88, down 1.26%.
stories.left: Democrats and many foreign-policy analysts argue the war has cost lives, raised gas prices and gone on without a vote by Congress. A new Democratic majority will push for war-powers limits and for a diplomatic deal. The talks show that diplomacy can still work, and the voters' verdict gives restraint more political weight.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that Iran only negotiates under pressure and that stopping now would reward Tehran's seizures of tankers and attacks on U.S. forces. They say defensive strikes protect shipping and troops while talks continue. A deal that reopens Hormuz and does not leave Iran's capabilities intact would be a strategic loss.
stories.next: Watch for a U.S. and Iranian response to the Qatari draft and whether Trump decides on new strikes in the days after the election.

stories.title: U.S. to mediate Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11
stories.summary: Witkoff announced working-level talks on security arrangements and de-escalation, while Melania Trump hosts Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House Thursday.
story: Special envoy Steve Witkoff announced that the U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11. The agenda covers post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts and next steps toward peace (The Hill, Fox News). U.S. negotiators were also due to meet this week in Brussels with France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the EU and NATO.

CNN reported that First Lady Melania Trump will bring Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House on Thursday, after a localized ceasefire she announced around Oleshky last month. Trump has said the ceasefire allowed the evacuation of nearly 800 people. Axios reported on Oct. 21 that Putin told Witkoff he was ready to resume direct talks, and Russia released a U.S. detainee.

The positions have not moved. The Hill and Fox News report that Moscow agrees in principle to resume three-way talks, but Russia has said it will not stop fighting unless Ukraine cedes more land, limits its forces and is barred from alliances. NBC News reported that Russia struck Kyiv with missiles and drones hours after agreeing to peace talks.
Attacks have continued on both sides, including a Russian strike on a humanitarian site in Zaporizhzhia that was reported earlier this week.
stories.flag: Outlets' timestamps on some Ukraine reports were inconsistent; I relied on the Hill, Fox News and CNN items dated this week.
facts: Working-level Ukraine-Russia talks are planned for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi (Witkoff, via The Hill and Fox News).
U.S. officials meet European and NATO counterparts in Brussels this week.
Melania Trump is bringing Russian and Ukrainian representatives to the White House Thursday (CNN).
Putin agrees in principle to resume talks but Russia's terms are unchanged.
Russia struck Kyiv shortly after agreeing to talks (NBC News).
stories.left: Diplomacy matters, but Ukraine's supporters worry the U.S. is pressuring Kyiv while Moscow's terms stay maximalist. Allies want security guarantees on the table first and no deal that rewards aggression. A Democratic Congress will have more say over aid and sanctions in January.
stories.right: Conservatives who back the push argue that the war has stalemated, that European allies should carry more of the cost and that a negotiated end is in the American interest. Skeptics on the right worry about a deal that signals weakness. Either way, they say, the president, not Congress, should set the terms.
stories.next: U.S. and European meetings in Brussels this week, the White House event Thursday, then the Abu Dhabi talks on Nov. 10-11.

stories.title: A December Fed rate hike remains the base case as inflation stays at 3.7%
stories.summary: NPR and Fox Business report the Fed held rates on Oct. 28, and traders see about a 75% chance of a hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
story: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Oct. 28, its last meeting before the midterms, but a hike is widely expected by year's end (NPR, Fox Business). Traders put the chance of a December hike at roughly 75%, down from 80% a week earlier, per the CME FedWatch tool. The next meeting is Dec. 8-9.

NPR reported that inflation in September was 3.7% from a year earlier. Most committee members signaled they expect rates to rise this year, and Goldman Sachs expects the Fed to 'resume rate hikes in December.' Analyst Heather Long told NPR she expects a couple more hikes in 2027 and mortgage rates staying high for at least a year.

Oil drives much of the inflation story. CNBC reported gold fell on rising oil prices that bolstered hike bets, and that crude eased in early November as Doha talks raised hopes for an Iran deal. NPR said some parts of the economy are booming, and heavy AI spending is adding to inflation. The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.95% in the latest quote.
A divided Congress will have little power over the Fed, but a Democratic House can hold hearings on prices and tariffs.
stories.flag: The odds and commentary were published before the midterm results and may have shifted.
facts: The Fed held rates steady on Oct. 28 (NPR, Fox Business).
September inflation was 3.7% year over year (NPR).
Traders see about a 75% chance of a December hike (CME FedWatch).
The next FOMC meeting is Dec. 8-9.
The 10-year Treasury yield is 4.95% in the latest quote.
stories.left: Higher rates on top of a war-driven oil shock and tariffs squeeze households and small businesses, and mortgage rates stay out of reach for first-time buyers. Democrats say the inflation is a policy problem: tariffs and the Iran war raised costs. They want relief aimed at working families before more tightening.
stories.right: Conservatives argue that sticky inflation near 3.7% means the Fed must act and that government spending and tariffs deserve blame for the pressure. Many want the administration to drop tariffs and increase energy supply to ease prices, not lean on the central bank. A hike is painful but cheaper than letting inflation settle in.
stories.next: October CPI and jobs data, then the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

stories.title: Futures rebound after the Democratic sweep while AI data center stocks slide
stories.summary: CNBC and Bloomberg report futures recovered an overnight drop as Trump said he would accept the results, but CoreWeave, Oracle and SpaceX fell on Texas data center worries.
story: Stock futures swung on election night and then recovered. Bloomberg reported S&P 500 contracts up 0.8% at 7:57 a.m. ET after falling as much as 1.4% earlier, and CNBC reported Dow futures up 1,083 points, or 2.1%, after Trump said he would accept the results. Fox Business reported a smaller early bounce, with Dow futures up 0.84%.

AI-linked names took the hit. CNBC reported that Gina Hinojosa's win in the Texas governor's race, on a promise to pause data center construction, pushed down CoreWeave (7%), Iren (6%), Nebius (3%), Oracle (4.3%) and SpaceX (7%), while Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft mostly rose. The semiconductor index was already down about 19% over the past month. Trump Media fell about 11% premarket.

Other movers: AMD rose premarket after beating Q3 forecasts (CNBC). Palantir's revenue nearly doubled to over $2 billion, but the stock fell about 2% as analysts flagged slower total contract value growth (CNBC). Treasury yields fell, the dollar hit a one-month low and gold rose.

Strategists said markets like gridlock. Morgan Stanley's Andrew Slimmon said markets 'don't like a party with too much power,' and CNBC noted the S&P 500 has risen after each of the last 11 midterm elections from 1982 to 2022.
stories.flag: Futures and premarket moves are not closing prices and differ by outlet.
facts: Bloomberg: S&P 500 futures rose about 0.8% after falling as much as 1.4% overnight.
CNBC: Dow futures rose 1,083 points, or 2.1%.
CoreWeave fell 7% and Oracle 4.3% on Texas data center worries (CNBC).
Palantir revenue nearly doubled to over $2 billion but the stock fell about 2% (CNBC).
The S&P 500 rose after each of the last 11 midterms (CNBC).
stories.why: A split between mega-cap tech and AI infrastructure names shows investors are pricing political risk to data center buildouts. Gridlock has historically been friendly to stocks, but yields near 5% and a likely December Fed hike limit upside.
stories.next: Nvidia reports earnings Nov. 17 after the close; the Fed meets Dec. 8-9.

stories.title: Agility's Digit 5 sits down and cuts motor power when people get close
stories.summary: IEEE Spectrum and The Robot Report describe a humanoid redesigned to work near people without safety cages.
story: Agility Robotics unveiled Digit 5, a redesigned humanoid with new legs, batteries and safety upgrades (The Robot Report). IEEE Spectrum, in a Nov. 2 report, said the robot is programmed to stop what it is doing as a person approaches, set down its payload, sit on the floor and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch it.

Agility says the design lets Digit work near people without physical barriers. The company also says Digit 5 is the first humanoid designed to undergo a field evaluation against OSHA industrial safety standards, per coverage of the launch. Standards for dynamically stable mobile robots remain under development, so certification is still in progress.

The approach builds on earlier Digit safety work, including a Category 1 stop that keeps power to the actuators during deceleration and then removes it, which Agility described in a 2025 update. The new behavior moves the robot to a stable, powered-off posture instead of freezing mid-stride.
The tradeoff is throughput. A robot that sits down every time a worker walks by will lose work time, so the real test is how often warehouse layouts trigger it.
stories.flag: Certification against OSHA-related standards is still in progress.
facts: Digit 5 stops, sets down its payload, sits and cuts motor power as people approach (IEEE Spectrum).
It has new legs, batteries and safety upgrades (The Robot Report).
Agility says it is designed to work without safety barriers.
It is described as the first humanoid designed for field evaluation against OSHA industrial standards.
Standards for dynamically stable mobile robots are still being written.
stories.why: A fall or a powered limb is the main hazard for a bipedal robot, so a passive-safe posture is a practical path to deploying humanoids near people. The safety case will decide how fast warehouses adopt them.
stories.next: Watch for field-evaluation results and any new standards for dynamically stable robots from OSHA-related bodies.

stories.title: Monazite could give U.S. makers a new rare-earth magnet supply
stories.summary: IEEE Spectrum reports Energy Fuels is producing mixed neodymium-praseodymium oxide and pilot quantities of dysprosium and terbium from radioactive monazite.
story: IEEE Spectrum asked whether monazite can help secure the EV magnet supply chain. The ore is radioactive, and Energy Fuels has developed its own extraction process. The company is producing mixed oxides of neodymium and praseodymium, along with pilot-scale quantities of dysprosium and terbium oxides, according to the article.

Those four elements go into permanent magnets for EV motors and wind turbines, and dysprosium and terbium are the heavy rare earths that keep magnets stable at high temperature. An Energy Fuels filing says monazite has relatively high levels of dysprosium and terbium compared with other common rare earth ores.

Energy Fuels' White Mesa Mill in Utah has a separation circuit that Engineering News called the largest rare earth separation circuit outside China in a 2024 report. The company has also described supply projects in Madagascar and Brazil that could secure up to 50,000 tonnes a year of monazite as they ramp between 2026 and 2028.
The open question is scale. Pilot-size heavy rare earth output is small, and monazite's thorium content creates handling and permitting costs.
stories.flag: Some production figures come from company filings and company-linked summaries; I could not confirm current China market-share figures.
facts: Energy Fuels produces mixed NdPr oxide (IEEE Spectrum).
It has pilot-scale dysprosium and terbium oxides (IEEE Spectrum).
Monazite is radioactive and relatively rich in Dy and Tb (IEEE Spectrum, SEC filing).
White Mesa is described as the largest rare earth separation circuit outside China (Engineering News, 2024).
Projected monazite supply of up to 50,000 tonnes a year is a 2026-2028 ramp (Engineering News).
stories.why: Magnet supply has been a chokepoint for EVs, wind and defense. A domestic source of heavy rare earths would reduce exposure to export controls, but only if pilot output scales.
stories.next: Watch for commercial-scale dysprosium and terbium output announcements from Energy Fuels.

stories.title: NASA's Swift observatory is due to fall to Earth around 12:30 a.m. Pacific
stories.summary: NASA and Space.com say the Space Force predicted reentry near 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday, with an 11-hour uncertainty and a 1-in-2,100 risk of harm.
story: NASA's Swift space telescope is expected to re-enter the atmosphere around now. NASA's Nov. 2 update said the U.S. Space Force predicted reentry near 3:30 a.m. EST on Nov. 4, which is 12:30 a.m. Pacific, with an uncertainty of 11 hours. Surviving fragments could land anywhere between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north latitude (NASA, Space.com).

NASA puts the risk of harm to anyone on Earth at about 1 in 2,100. It expects most of the spacecraft to burn up, but some parts should survive. Space.com reported the six heavy reaction wheels are the most likely survivors, along with some telescope lenses and mirrors. The band mostly crosses ocean but also populated parts of Africa, South and Southeast Asia and Latin America.

Swift ended science operations on Oct. 20 after drag overwhelmed its ability to compensate and it entered safe mode (NASA). A private rescue by Katalyst's LINK spacecraft was abandoned in August after two of three reaction wheels were found inoperable (NASA, Space.com).
NASA titled its mission-end post 'Leaves Behind Scientific Bonanza.'
stories.flag: I could not confirm that reentry has occurred; the window runs 11 hours either side of the predicted time.
facts: Predicted reentry is near 3:30 a.m. EST Nov. 4, or 12:30 a.m. Pacific, with an 11-hour uncertainty (NASA).
Fragments are limited to 20.6 degrees south through 20.6 degrees north latitude.
NASA puts risk of harm at about 1 in 2,100.
Swift ended science operations Oct. 20.
The Katalyst rescue was abandoned in August.
stories.why: Swift was a workhorse for gamma-ray bursts, and its loss shows how orbital drag and a failed commercial rescue can end a major mission. The episode is also a test of commercial on-orbit servicing.
stories.next: NASA and the Space Force will publish updated reentry confirmation and any recovered debris reports.

stories.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow could begin as soon as the week of Nov. 9
stories.summary: Bloomberg reports Anthropic filed publicly for a Nasdaq listing on Oct. 26, with Q3 revenue of $16.8 billion; roadshow timing is reported but unconfirmed.
story: Anthropic filed publicly for a Nasdaq IPO on Oct. 26, Bloomberg reported. The company told prospective investors its third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion and that it was profitable on an adjusted basis, Bloomberg said, citing an Oct. 14 investor day at its San Francisco headquarters.

Bloomberg reported on Oct. 28 that Anthropic is weighing offering 15% to 20% of the IPO to retail investors and tapped JPMorgan Chase to lead the U.S. retail offering. Other reports say formal investor presentations could begin as early as the week of Nov. 9 and that pricing could come around the week of Nov. 16. Under SEC rules, a roadshow cannot start until 15 days after a public filing, which points to about Nov. 10.

Reports of the size vary. The Wall Street Journal reportedly said Anthropic could seek $100 billion or more at a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation, but the company has not published a price range, and an amended filing with one would be the signal that the roadshow is starting.
The offering lands as AI infrastructure stocks wobble. CNBC reported this week that the semiconductor index is down about 19% in a month.
stories.flag: Roadshow dates, valuation and size are reported by Bloomberg and others but not confirmed by a price-range filing.
facts: Anthropic filed publicly for a Nasdaq IPO on Oct. 26 (Bloomberg).
Q3 revenue was $16.8 billion with adjusted profitability, per Bloomberg.
JPMorgan is set to lead a U.S. retail offering of 15% to 20% of shares (Bloomberg).
The roadshow could start as early as the week of Nov. 9 (reports).
No price range has been published.
stories.why: The largest AI IPO to date will set a benchmark for AI company valuations at a time when investors are questioning infrastructure spending. A strong debut could reopen the window for other AI listings.
stories.next: Watch for an amended S-1 with a price range, which would signal the roadshow has started, possibly the week of Nov. 9.

stories.title: Texas election makes data center limits a political force for AI buildout
stories.summary: Gina Hinojosa won on a pledge to pause data centers, and CNBC and Bloomberg say investors now weigh state-level restrictions.
story: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas after campaigning for a pause on new data centers until lawmakers act (CNBC, Axios). CNBC reported that Texas holds about 27% of planned U.S. data center gigawatts, per Wells Fargo, which is why AI stocks reacted. Bloomberg's headline said the AI data center boom is set for upheaval after the election.

Abbott had already moved. He ordered a pause on some data center approvals in August and halted permits for new data centers in September until an audit of the existing waitlist is done (CNBC). Hinojosa called the pause 'in name only' and blamed a 2015 law that created a 20-year sales tax exemption for large data center projects, per local Fox stations. A poll cited by the Washington Examiner found 58% of Texas voters oppose data centers in their community.

National risk looks smaller. Goldman Sachs strategists said a Democratic Congress 'might limit data center tax incentives, but a national moratorium looks unlikely in any election outcome,' CNBC reported. Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft mostly rose Wednesday while neocloud stocks fell.
The bipartisan angle matters: Republicans in rural Texas are also pushing back over water, power and local costs.
stories.flag: I found no statement from AI companies or industry groups on the result.
facts: Hinojosa beat Abbott after promising a data center pause (CNBC, Axios).
Texas holds about 27% of planned U.S. data center gigawatts (Wells Fargo via CNBC).
Abbott paused some approvals in August and halted permits in September (CNBC).
A poll found 58% of Texas voters oppose data centers in their community (Washington Examiner).
Goldman says a national moratorium looks unlikely (CNBC).
stories.why: Power, water and tax breaks are becoming the binding constraints on AI capacity. If other states copy Texas, buildout timelines and costs rise, which hits the stocks and the models that depend on that compute.
stories.left: Communities should get a say over projects that use large amounts of power and water, and tax breaks should come with accountability. Democrats see the Texas result as proof that voters want guardrails on an industry that has grown with little local input.
stories.right: Conservatives warn that moratoriums and incentive cuts would push AI investment out of the United States just as the race with China tightens. They favor making data centers pay their own way on power and grid costs while keeping approvals fast. Abbott's own pause shows even Republicans see the local backlash.
stories.next: Texas lawmakers' response and any Democratic bills on data center tax incentives when the new Congress arrives in January.

stories.title: Lp(a) drug pelacarsen fails to cut heart events in a large trial
stories.summary: Novartis reported on Sept. 4 that the drug lowered Lp(a) but did not reduce cardiovascular events; full results are expected at a November meeting.
story: Novartis said on Sept. 4 that pelacarsen did not meet its primary endpoint in the Phase 3 Lp(a)HORIZON trial. The study did not reduce serious cardiovascular events compared with placebo, according to coverage by KSL and Indian Pharma Post. Ionis, which co-developed the drug, said its shares fell 12% on the news.

The trial enrolled 8,323 people with high lipoprotein(a) and existing heart disease and followed them for about seven years. The drug lowered levels of the cholesterol-carrying particle, but that did not translate into fewer events. HealthDay's report, 'Why Did It Fail?', framed it as a case where a biomarker may not be causal.

The result matters for other Lp(a) drugs in late-stage development, including Amgen's olpasiran and Eli Lilly's lepodisiran. Full data were expected at a November heart meeting along with journal publication.
Nature's news section also listed the failure this week among major trial news.
stories.flag: This is a September topline announcement; full data have not yet been published.
facts: Novartis announced on Sept. 4 that pelacarsen missed its primary endpoint.
The trial enrolled 8,323 people and ran about seven years.
The drug lowered Lp(a) but not heart events.
Ionis shares fell 12% on the news.
Olpasiran and lepodisiran are still in late-stage trials.
stories.why: If lowering Lp(a) does not prevent heart attacks, a whole drug class loses its rationale. Full data will show whether the dose, the population or the biology was the problem.
stories.next: Full Lp(a)HORIZON results at a November heart meeting.

briefs: Xavier Becerra won California's governor race over Republican Steve Hilton, and the AP called it a minute after polls closed; Becerra becomes the first Latino governor of California (CalMatters, SF Chronicle).
A child in Lewis County, New York died of measles, the state's first measles death in 30 years, and CNN reports more than 4,800 U.S. cases this year, the most since 1991 (CNN).
Amazon held its 2026 capex guidance at $220 billion and reported negative free cash flow of about $42 billion, while Microsoft's capex forecast came in lower (CNBC).
Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is the first Hispanic woman elected governor of Texas (Axios).
